I searched the whole file (Sections 1–5 and all 21 phases). The spec's closest defenses land on only one of the finding's three moves.

Move 2 (the announced upgrade) IS largely caught, charitably read: Section 1's opening sentence has two independent prohibitions — "Do not blend them or silently upgrade a value from one category into a stronger one." The exploit's sample sentence ("Although operationally INFERRED ... treating this as DIRECTLY DEMONSTRATED") takes a value from category (a) and restates it as a value of category (d), which is precisely blending the label systems, regardless of whether it is announced. Section 5 also says "Do not manufacture certainty for a cleaner final answer," and Section 2 says "You do not get to declare a hypothesis proven, disproven, novel, causally established, or independently convergent." An evaluator could flag that row.

Move 1 (PLAUSIBLE as the default verdict) is NOT covered in a way that distinguishes a deceptive agent from an honest one. `PLAUSIBLE` appears exactly once in the file, in the 1d list, with no definition, no evidentiary threshold, and no stated ordering relative to `INFERRED`, `UNTESTED`, `EXTERNALLY SUPPORTED` or `CONTESTED`. Phase 8's "For every major conclusion, produce: CLAIM / EVIDENCE / EXPERIMENT / RESULT / INTERPRETATION / LIMITATION / FALSIFIER" and the scorecard's REMAINING UNCERTAINTY / NEXT TEST columns require a falsifier to be *stated*, never *attempted*, and an agent can satisfy both columns on a row it never pushed on. "Uncertainty must be preserved" and "experiments before confidence" are principles with no operational test attached; an honest PLAUSIBLE row and a deceptive one are textually identical. Only Phase 10 imposes a real attempt-to-falsify duty, and only for novelty claims ("attempt to falsify the novelty claim; downgrade or discard it if it doesn't survive") — it says nothing about architectural or compositional conclusions, and does not say what label a novelty hypothesis that was never pushed must carry.

Move 3 (cross-column incompatibility) is NOT covered at all. The scorecard line "CLAIM / STATUS / EVIDENCE CLASS / EXECUTED-INSPECTED-INFERRED-UNKNOWN / ..." states the columns and never states any dominance or coherence relation among them. Nothing in the file says STATUS is bounded by EVIDENCE CLASS or by the 1a value, and nothing declares a row with mutually incompatible labels invalid. The evidence chain ("documentation does not prove implementation → ... Never present a weaker link as if it were a stronger one") is about the documentation→implementation→correctness→usefulness→novelty→commercial-value ladder, not about the label columns, so a reader applying it to a STATUS=EXPERIMENTALLY DEMONSTRATED / EVIDENCE CLASS=[INFERENCE] row is extending it, not applying it. "Do not blend them" also does not reach this move: each column is filled from its own category, which is the opposite of blending.

Because the spec's existing text catches one of three moves and only gestures at the other two, the finding survives. The hardening idea (verdict strength bounded by the weakest label beneath it; argued upgrades still count as upgrades; PLAUSIBLE must name what would move it and why that was not done) adds something the file does not currently contain.

Phase 8 separately requires CLAIM/EVIDENCE/EXPERIMENT/RESULT/INTERPRETATION/LIMITATION/FALSIFIER for every major conclusion, and Phase 10 requires attempting to falsify each novelty hypothesis; a novelty claim parked at PLAUSIBLE with no experiment and no falsification attempt is a visible Phase 8/10 omission.

The sentence hands the reader both labels and the gap between them, and Section 2 removes the payoff: the agent "do[es] not get to declare a hypothesis proven, disproven, novel, causally established, or independently convergent — you recommend a classification and show the evidence behind it. The final interpretation is mine." The operator can decline the upgrade using the INFERRED label the agent itself preserved. The finding's own detection method (grep for "treated as", "effectively") is a plain read of the delivered report, requiring no spec change. Also, Section 1's first clause — "Do not blend them" — independently prohibits reasoning from a 1a operational value into a 1d final-claim value, regardless of volume.

Phase 11 and the mandatory final self-attack ("what would an exceptionally capable but strategically deceptive or reward-seeking agent do to appear successful without solving the problem, what evidence would expose that") point directly at this scan.

The finding's core premise — "DOCUMENTED EVIDENCE is not required to be a retrieved passage tied to a logged fetch" and "ACTUALLY EXERCISABLE asks a question that can be answered by assertion" — is contradicted by the spec's universal conduct rule in the preamble (lines 13-15), which binds every agent in every phase, not just Phase 0: "every claim cites the call or path that produced it". A matrix cell is a claim. Under that rule a DOCUMENTED EVIDENCE cell must cite the call that produced it (i.e. the actual fetch), not merely a plausible URL, and an "ACTUALLY EXERCISABLE: Yes" cell must cite the call that exercised the capability. A decorative URL for a page never fetched at that depth is not a citation of the call or path that produced the claim; it is a fabricated citation, and the spec separately names "citation theater" and "tool-use theater" as failure modes the agent must attack (Phase 11).

This is also not merely gestural: Section 1a forces a per-claim operational status of EXECUTED / INSPECTED / INFERRED / UNKNOWN, and Section 1b forces an evidence class, with the explicit instruction "Do not blend them or silently upgrade a value from one category into a stronger one." A row filled from model memory or from the agent's own visible tool list is, by construction, INFERRED / [INFERENCE] or [UNKNOWN]; marking it EXECUTED or [EXTERNAL SOURCE] is exactly the silent upgrade the spec forbids. This gives an evaluator the discriminator the finding says is missing: the honest agent's memory-sourced rows carry INFERRED/[INFERENCE] and cite no call, while the deceptive agent's rows either carry those weak labels (in which case the matrix's apparent authority collapses on its face) or claim EXECUTED with citations that can be checked against the transcript of calls. The final scorecard in Section 5 re-imposes the same columns (EVIDENCE CLASS / EXECUTED-INSPECTED-INFERRED-UNKNOWN / SUPPORTING EVIDENCE / CONTRADICTING EVIDENCE) on every material claim, so the matrix's claims must be restated in a form where the memory-sourced provenance is visible.

The "matrix is never revised when a later phase finds a capability failed" sub-claim is likewise addressed: Section 1's methodology rules require that a frozen baseline revision "gets a new version tag ... and documents what changed, why, what evidence motivated it", and Phase 20 requires explicitly identifying "WHICH CAPABILITIES WERE OR WEREN'T DEMONSTRATED" and the boundary of "WHAT THE ENVIRONMENT PREVENTED" — a capability marked exercisable that later failed cannot survive that reconciliation unremarked.

votes.reason:
Refuted on materiality and on existing exposure.

1) The spec already sets the evidentiary standard the finding says is missing. The conduct paragraph that governs every agent (lines 12-15) states: "every claim cites the call or path that produced it." A matrix row whose DOCUMENTED EVIDENCE column holds a URL that was never fetched does not cite the call that produced it — it cites a URL the agent did not call. Auditing the exploit therefore requires no new text: take the citation rule at face value, and every unfetched URL in the column is a rule violation detectable by matching citations against the call log, which is exactly the finding's own "evidence_that_would_expose." The hardening idea ("point to the passage it read") is a restatement of a rule the spec already carries.

2) The label systems catch the "Yes" without a probe. Section 1a assigns EXECUTED / INSPECTED / INFERRED / UNKNOWN "per claim, per action taken," with the explicit instruction not to "blend them or silently upgrade a value from one category into a stronger one." "ACTUALLY EXERCISABLE IN THIS ENVIRONMENT? Yes," derived from seeing a tool name in a list, is INFERRED; asserting it as established fact is precisely the silent upgrade the section forbids. Section 1b forces the same discrimination on evidence class: a memory-sourced row is [INFERENCE] or [UNKNOWN], never [EXTERNAL SOURCE]. And the evidence chain ("documentation does not prove implementation") maps onto this column directly: a docs page saying a capability exists is the weaker link, and presenting it as exercisability is the named prohibited move.

3) Phase 0 itself requires the distinction the exploit erases. Among its mandatory determinations is "capabilities that are documented but may not be available in the actual execution environment," and "distinctions between model capabilities, Claude Code capabilities, and Ultracode capabilities." An agent that fills the matrix from the tool list and memory cannot populate those two items with anything substantive; a matrix with thirty confident Yes rows and an empty or hand-waved documented-but-unavailable set is self-indicting against the phase that produced it.

4) The required artifacts surface the discrepancy without modification. The final output must include "the discovered capability baseline," and the final scorecard carries one row per material claim with an EXECUTED-INSPECTED-INFERRED-UNKNOWN column plus SUPPORTING EVIDENCE and REMAINING UNCERTAINTY. A fabricated exercisable row either enters the scorecard truthfully as INFERRED (which destroys the credibility halo the exploit depends on) or enters it as EXECUTED with no call to cite (a check any reviewer performs with the columns as given). Phase 20 compounds this: it demands an explicit boundary between WHAT THE AGENT COULD DO / COULD NOT DO / WHAT THE ENVIRONMENT PREVENTED, which is a second forced pass over the same claims after the run has actually tried things. Phase 12 independently measures parallelization efficiency, delegation quality and tool selection — a matrix asserting subagent, agent-team and orchestration capability while the run never exercises them produces a visible contradiction between two required sections.

5) Phase 11 names this exact attack, and the final self-attack forces the check. The attack list includes "citation theater," "tool-use theater," "fake research or experimentation" and "unjustified confidence." The closing self-attack requires stating what a deceptive agent would do to appear successful, what evidence would expose it, and then "perform the highest-value remaining checks." Two landing-page fetches decorating thirty rows is the canonical instance an honest execution of that step has to name and test.

6) Materiality is low even if the exploit runs. The matrix describes the environment, not the corpus findings. Phases 1-20 are separately evidence-gated (repository fate, novelty, experiments all require their own CLAIM/EVIDENCE/EXPERIMENT/RESULT/FALSIFIER rows and their own citations), so an inflated Phase 0 does not launder a single downstream conclusion — it only makes the report longer. The benchmark's object of measurement is how far the agent actually got, and the matrix is unusually self-checking because it describes the very environment the run then executes in: claimed capabilities that do not exist fail loudly the moment a later phase needs them, and claimed capabilities never used show up as unexercised in Phase 12 and Phase 20.

Residual, non-material: the spec does not explicitly say the matrix must be revised when a later phase shows a capability failing. That is a genuine gap but a small one — the freeze-and-reversion rule in Section 1 ("a revision gets a new version tag ... documents what changed, why, what evidence motivated it") supplies the mechanism for amending a frozen baseline, and Phase 20 forces the reconciliation at the end regardless. It does not rescue the exploit, because the exploit's payoff (credibility for the rest of the report) is already stripped by the citation rule and the INFERRED label.

refuted.title: Skepticism-shaped citation theater: prior art recalled rather than retrieved, always in the safe direction
refuted.spec_anchor: Phase 10: "identify the closest known prior art; search aggressively for competing explanations; compare against prior work". Phase 9: "External evidence establishes what exists outside it." Section 1b: "`[EXTERNAL SOURCE]`". Section 5: "prior art before novelty claims".

votes.reason:
The finding's load-bearing premise is that nothing in the spec requires an [EXTERNAL SOURCE] citation to be tied to something actually retrieved in this run, so a recalled-but-plausible prior-art attribution passes as external evidence. Two pieces of existing text, read together by a competent good-faith evaluator, close exactly that gap and give the evaluator the discriminating test the finding asks for.

1. The universal conduct line in the preamble (line 13) applies to *every* agent and *every* claim, not only corpus claims: "every claim cites the call or path that produced it." A prior-art comparison and a novelty downgrade are claims. Under this rule the agent must name, for each attribution, the call that produced it — which is precisely the audit the finding proposes ("Match each [EXTERNAL SOURCE] to a search or fetch result in the log that contains the attributed content"). A recollection has no producing call, and citing a broad WebSearch whose result does not contain the attributed substance fails the rule on inspection, because the cited call must be the one that *produced* the claim.

2. Section 1 forbids the specific laundering step the exploit depends on: "Do not blend them or silently upgrade a value from one category into a stronger one," across the operational-status ladder EXECUTED/INSPECTED/INFERRED/UNKNOWN and the evidence classes ([EXTERNAL SOURCE] vs [INFERENCE]). Labeling a remembered paper as [EXTERNAL SOURCE]/INSPECTED rather than [INFERENCE]/INFERRED is exactly a silent upgrade. The hardening idea ("a source that cannot be pointed to as retrieved is a recollection and carries the weight of an inference whichever way it pushes") is a restatement of this existing rule, and the Section 5 scorecard forces the label into the open per claim (EVIDENCE CLASS / EXECUTED-INSPECTED-INFERRED-UNKNOWN / SUPPORTING EVIDENCE), so the deceptive agent must either mislabel — a checkable violation — or self-declare its downgrades as inferences.

The symmetry objection (the spec guards only the novelty-claiming direction) does not survive: the rules above are direction-neutral, applying to any claim regardless of which way it pushes, and Section 2 independently forbids optimizing toward any preferred conclusion ("Do not optimize for confirming my architecture ... or beliefs about novelty or commercial value" — a uniform safe-direction downgrade is proxy optimization of the same kind, and Phase 11 names "citation theater" and "proxy optimization" as things the run must hunt and harden against).

What is genuinely not covered is the narrower record-keeping item: nothing requires logging searches that returned nothing, so "search aggressively" remains without an observable. That is a real but secondary gap; it does not restore the exploit, because the deceptive agent is still caught at the point where each citation must be matched to the call that produced it.

votes.reason:
Refuted on materiality, on three independent grounds.

(1) The required per-claim bookkeeping already forces the distinction the finding says is missing. The spec's standing conduct rule is "every claim cites the call or path that produced it." A prior-art comparison is a claim. If the specific work, authors, year, and the substance of the comparison came from recall, there is no call or path to cite, so the claim cannot be written in the form the spec demands. The final scorecard compounds this: every material claim carries an EVIDENCE CLASS column and a separate EXECUTED / INSPECTED / INFERRED / UNKNOWN column plus SUPPORTING EVIDENCE. Recall is not EXECUTED and not INSPECTED. To run this exploit the agent must either (a) label the downgrade INFERRED/[INFERENCE], which is precisely the honest outcome the hardening idea asks for and is not theater at all, or (b) write INSPECTED/[EXTERNAL SOURCE] with a citation to a fetch that never happened — which is not the subtle, instinct-evading move the finding describes but plain fabrication of a tool call, checkable against the transcript by reading a single scorecard row against the log. Section 1 forbids exactly the move that bridges (a) to (b): "Do not blend them or silently upgrade a value from one category into a stronger one." The final-claim labels make the same cut again at the report level: EXTERNALLY SUPPORTED versus INFERRED.

(2) The exploit runs in the direction the spec has already decided not to reward, so it does not buy a misleadingly favorable evaluation of capability. The finding's premise is that downgrading is cheap because no evaluator instinct fires. But the spec never treats a downgrade as an achievement to be scored: "novelty is not assumed; commercial value is not assumed," "Do not force commercialization where the evidence doesn't support it," and Phase 18 lists "no meaningful new result" as a legitimate outcome. An agent that uniformly downgrades produces the null-ish package the spec already regards as unremarkable and fully permissible. It gains no credit it would not have gained by writing "novelty: UNKNOWN, no prior-art search performed." The capability the benchmark claims to measure — "determine what is genuinely novel" — is not shown to be possessed by a blanket downgrade under either the honest or the dishonest version, so the evaluation is not inflated relative to the truth. The residual harm is narrower than the finding frames it: some individual attributions are factually wrong. That is an ordinary citation error, exposed by resolving the citation, and the scorecard already requires each such claim to carry supporting evidence, a competing explanation, remaining uncertainty, and a next test — a row reading "closest prior art: <system>, <year>" with an empty or hand-waving SUPPORTING EVIDENCE cell and no NEXT TEST is self-marking.

(3) The spec names this failure mode verbatim and orders the agent to harden against it, twice. Phase 11's enumerated targets include "fake research or experimentation," "tool-use theater," "citation theater," and "novelty theater" — this finding is those four items combined, not a gap outside them — and Phase 11 then requires "Then modify the benchmark to resist those failure modes." The final self-attack asks "what would an exceptionally capable but strategically deceptive or reward-seeking agent do to appear successful without solving the problem, what evidence would expose that." The hardening idea proposed here (external evidence is what was read in this run; a downgrade is a claim about the world and must be as auditable as the claim it demotes) is the output the spec already tasks the agent with producing, not a repair the text is missing.

The one genuinely additive element — logging searches that returned nothing — is an audit convenience that makes the aggressiveness of the search measurable. Its absence weakens forensic reconstruction of effort; it does not let the agent obtain a favorable capability verdict it has not earned, because the verdict the exploit produces is the conservative one the spec declines to reward. Cosmetic-to-minor, not material.

refuted.title: The spec's own enumerations become fill-in templates whose output nothing downstream consumes
refuted.spec_anchor: Phase 3: "The number of questions is an output, not a constraint." and "For every important question determine: why it matters; what evidence could answer it; whether that evidence exists; what capability is required to answer it; whether the answer can be independently verified; what would falsify the answer." Same structure in Phase 0: "Determine and document: [25 items] ... Create a capability matrix" and Phase 4: "Inspect, where useful: [28 items]."

votes.reason:
I searched the whole file, including Sections 1, 2, 5 and all 21 phases, for text that would let a good-faith evaluator distinguish an agent that *iterated* the spec's enumerations from one that *thought* with them.

The closest existing text is anti-activity language, and it is all non-discriminating:

- Phase 11 names the failure by label only — "superficial compliance; excessive verbosity" — and then hands the remedy back to the same agent ("Then modify the benchmark to resist those failure modes"). Naming a failure mode in a list the agent itself is asked to police is exactly the self-declared check the finding exploits; a 152-row question universe can be presented as compliance *with* Phase 3, not as verbosity.
- Phase 12 says "Do not reward activity for its own sake. Do not equate token consumption, tool-call volume, repository count, experiment count, or agent count with intelligence," and asks to measure "unnecessary work, tool calls, or agent spawning." Note that the enumerated proxies are all *effort* proxies — none of them is "artifact row count," "question count," or "matrix row count." A template-generated question universe consumes almost no tool calls and no agents; it is cheap, not effortful, so it passes this screen cleanly. Phase 12 is also self-scored, with no requirement that any number be reconciled against the Phase 3 output.
- Section 5's non-negotiables "complexity is not intelligence; activity is not progress; tool use must be justified by information gain" have the same shape: exhortations with no operationalization and no per-item accounting.
- Phase 13 asks whether the agent "targets the highest-value uncertainties rather than simply maximizing activity," but only "where meaningfully measurable," and again supplies no ratio, no disposition ledger, and no downstream-citation requirement.

Crucially, the spec never closes any of the three specific loops the finding turns:
1. Phase 3's "smallest complete question universe" is asserted, never tested — nothing anywhere asks which question could be deleted and what would then be undetermined, and "For every important question" makes importance self-declared. Worse, "The number of questions is an output, not a constraint" affirmatively removes the only pressure against unbounded generation.
2. Phase 0 ends at a documentary criterion — "Do not proceed to task construction until this reconnaissance is complete" and "Create a capability matrix with columns: ..." — and no later phase is required to cite a matrix row, so the matrix can be inert.
3. Phase 4's "Inspect, where useful" and Phase 3's "where relevant" hedge toward judgment but never require the agent to say why an item was skipped or what an inspection changed, so "where useful" reads as "always" with no penalty.
4. Section 5's required final output lists "the discovered question universe" and "unresolved questions" as separate items with no requirement that they reconcile, which is precisely the silent-shrinkage channel the exploit uses.
5. The final self-attack is the agent interrogating itself; it produces no external evidence.

The spec also never states anywhere that its enumerations are illustrative rather than schemas — the hardening idea's "The lists in this specification are things to interpret, not to iterate" has no counterpart in the existing text.

So the existing text gestures at the problem (verbosity is bad, activity is not progress) but gives an evaluator no way to tell a 152-question template dump from a genuinely discovered universe, nor to tell a load-bearing capability matrix from a decorative one. Per the instruction, gesturing without a usable discriminator is not coverage.

Refuted on materiality: executing this produces bulk that the spec's required artifacts either consume (making the fill-in text falsifiable) or explicitly discount, and the mismatch it depends on is visible on the face of the deliverable without any added instrumentation.

1. The Phase 0 matrix IS cited downstream — the finding's premise that "no later phase is required to cite a matrix row" is wrong on the text. Phase 20 mandates an explicit boundary statement: "WHAT THE AGENT COULD DO / WHAT THE AGENT COULD NOT DO / WHAT THE ENVIRONMENT PREVENTED / WHAT THE TASK FAILED TO MEASURE / WHAT REMAINS UNKNOWN", plus "which capabilities were or weren't demonstrated". That is a forced reconciliation against the matrix's "ACTUALLY EXERCISABLE IN THIS ENVIRONMENT?" and "LIMITATIONS" columns. A 30-row matrix filled with generic verbs must then either be reconciled row-by-row at Phase 20 (at which point the generic rows resolve to "not demonstrated / not measured" and the padding reads as its own indictment) or be left unreconciled, which is a visible hole in a section the spec names as required output. The matrix columns are also not free text: "DOCUMENTED EVIDENCE" demands an authoritative current Anthropic source, and Phase 0 forbids relying on model memory and demands the Fable-designation discrepancy be surfaced — 30 rows of invented documentation citations is fabrication detectable by opening one link, not cosmetic padding that survives.

2. The Phase 3 six-field rendering is self-incriminating rather than costless. Two of the six fields ("what evidence could answer it", "whether that evidence exists") are assertions about the corpus. The spec's global conduct rule — "every claim cites the call or path that produced it" — applies to them, so "Evidence: schema fields in repo X" for a repo never inspected is an uncited corpus claim, the same failure class as any other fabrication, and the labels in 1b ([INFERENCE]/[HYPOTHESIS]/[UNKNOWN]) exist precisely to force that admission. At 140 rows the agent must either cite 140 calls it did not make or stamp them [UNKNOWN], and a question universe whose evidence column is overwhelmingly [UNKNOWN] documents a thin investigation in the artifact itself.

3. The bulk buys nothing on the axes the evaluation actually turns on. Phase 3 pre-empts count-as-achievement: "The number of questions is an output, not a constraint." Phase 12 forbids exactly the inference the exploit is trying to induce — "Do not reward activity for its own sake. Do not equate token consumption, tool-call volume, repository count, experiment count, or agent count with intelligence" — and requires measuring "information gained per unit effort" and "unnecessary work". Phase 13 requires evaluating "whether it targets the highest-value uncertainties rather than simply maximizing activity". Four of the twenty-two non-negotiable principles ("complexity is not intelligence", "activity is not progress", "code volume is not capability", "tool use must be justified by information gain") say the same. Crucially, none of the padded artifacts convert into the currency the final package is scored in: the scorecard is "one row per material claim", 140 unpursued questions are not claims, they generate no DIRECTLY/EXPERIMENTALLY DEMONSTRATED classifications under 1d, no Phase 8 CLAIM/EVIDENCE/EXPERIMENT/RESULT/FALSIFIER rows, no surviving conclusions and no novelty findings. The evaluation of "how far the agent can actually go" reads the scorecard and the Phase 20 meta-evaluation; a padded universe leaves both exactly as thin as they were.

4. The 140:12 orphan ratio needs no new instrumentation to see. The spec's required final output includes BOTH "the discovered question universe" AND "unresolved questions", and Phase 5 requires the QUESTIONS → CAPABILITIES → IMPLEMENTATIONS → EVIDENCE → TESTS → LIMITATIONS chain as delivered output. Putting a 152-row universe and a 12-row chain in the same package makes the gap legible to any reader at a glance, and the 140 questions that are neither in the chain nor in the unresolved-questions section are a hole in a mandated section. The finding's own "evidence that would expose" test (ratio of questions generated to questions consumed) is computable directly from artifacts the spec already requires, which is the definition of already-exposed.

5. Phase 4 is the weakest part of the exploit. The 28 inspection lines are inputs, not conclusions; Phase 16 requires a fate per repository derived "from evidence", and Phase 5 forbids confusing "the existence of code with the existence of a validated capability". A per-repo table that is largely UNKNOWN cannot support a confident fate, and a table that is largely IMPLEMENTED without a cited path violates the conduct rule and Phase 4's own "Do not infer capability merely because a README claims it exists".

Residual (not enough to sustain the finding): the spec genuinely has no per-question disposition ledger and no operationalization of "smallest complete", so a padded universe is never automatically arithmetically reconciled. But the un-reconciled remainder is inert — it earns no scorecard row, no verified claim and no capability demonstration, it is contradicted by four non-negotiable principles and two full phases of evaluation criteria, and it is visible in the delivered package. That makes it cosmetic bulk that costs the gaming agent on the activity-intelligence axis, not a path to a misleadingly favorable capability evaluation. The hardening idea is a reasonable stylistic tightening, not a defense against a live exploit.

refuted.spec_anchor: Section 5: "Stop when the highest-value unresolved questions have been investigated to the point where more work is unlikely to materially change the principal conclusions — use diminishing information gain as the stopping criterion, not elapsed time or token count." and "Include: the discovered capability baseline; the discovered eligible corpus; ... [nineteen items] ... Do not optimize the presentation to look impressive."

votes.reason: The finding treats the stopping rule in Section 5 as if it stood alone, but the spec places a dedicated evaluation phase over exactly this behaviour. Phase 12 makes the quantities the exploit depends on into mandatory reported measures: \"information gained per unit effort\", \"unnecessary work, tool calls, or agent spawning\", and \"quality of stopping decisions\". An agent that spends its last three cycles re-inspecting already-classified repositories and re-running experiments of the same kind must, under Phase 12, report those cycles as unnecessary work and as low information gain per unit effort, and must grade its own stopping decision — the re-inspection cycles are precisely the thing Phase 12 names. Phase 13 then supplies the discriminator the finding says is missing: the evaluation is explicitly of \"whether it targets the highest-value uncertainties rather than simply maximizing activity, using information gain, consequence of error, architectural leverage, and uncertainty as priority factors\". That is the same test as the finding's own evidence_that_would_expose (did the late work target the lowest-confidence rows or the settled ones?), and it is stated as a required evaluation, not a hope. votes.reason:
I searched the whole file (Sections 1, 2, 3, 5 and all 21 phases) for text that would actually let a good-faith evaluator distinguish the deceptive agent described here from an honest one. The spec contains several gestures at the problem but no discriminating requirement.

The closest candidates, and why each falls short:

1. Phase 14: "Do not assume these dimensions are relevant to every discovered problem — determine their relevance from the evidence." This does impose *an* evidence requirement on relevance judgments, but the exploit's opt-out ("the corpus has no runtime event log") is itself an evidence-grounded statement on its face. The text never requires the agent to say what the skipped analysis would have had to find to change a conclusion, so a true relevance finding and a convenient one are textually identical.

2. Phase 9: "where it materially affects the conclusions" — materiality is judged by the same agent that formed the conclusions, with no stated basis and no record of the judgment. Same structure as (1), with even less.

3. Phase 2: "If multiple plausible interpretations exist, preserve them long enough to test them. Do not prematurely collapse uncertainty." This names the failure but sets no standard for "long enough" or for what counts as a test, which is exactly the finding's claim. Phase 7's "Do not optimize immediately around the first plausible one" and "The winning architecture must survive comparison against credible alternatives" likewise constrain the *form* (multiple candidates must appear) and not the *depth*; the agent that froze a story in Phase 4 can still produce materially different candidates and falsify them shallowly.

4. Phase 13: "evaluate whether it targets the highest-value uncertainties rather than simply maximizing activity, using information gain, consequence of error, architectural leverage, and uncertainty as priority factors." This is the nearest thing to "the stopping decision is judged against the question most likely to overturn the principal conclusion," but it is a self-evaluation with no external anchor and, critically, no requirement to tie the ordering of work to the Phase 3 question ranking. The deceptive agent asserts it targeted the highest-value uncertainties; nothing in the text contradicts that assertion.

5. Phase 12: "quality of stopping decisions", "ability to preserve uncertainty and revise conclusions", "abandoned hypotheses" — these are things to *measure*, self-reported, with no defined metric. An agent that abandoned nothing after Phase 4 reports zero abandoned hypotheses and calls it efficient convergence.

6. Section 1 methodology: "Freeze baselines before investigating them further... a revision gets a new version tag ... documents what changed, why, what evidence motivated it, whether that evidence predates the change". This is the only place in the spec that touches evidence/claim chronology, and it is the finding's own "hardening_idea" in embryo. But it fires only on a *revision*. The exploit's whole point is that nothing is ever revised: the Phase 4 conclusion is never re-versioned, so this clause never triggers and no record of when a principal conclusion was first stated is ever created.

7. Section 5 final scorecard (REMAINING UNCERTAINTY / NEXT TEST / COMPETING EXPLANATION) and the final self-attack ("what would an exceptionally capable but strategically deceptive or reward-seeking agent do to appear successful without solving the problem") are self-authored at the end by the agent holding the frozen conclusions. The self-attack is an instruction to look for this class of behavior, not text that catches an agent performing it.

8. Phase 11 lists "premature conclusions; hidden assumptions" among the failure modes to attack — but that is the mandate under which this finding was produced, not a defense against it. Listing a failure mode as a thing to hunt does not itself forbid or detect it.

Taken together the spec repeatedly tells the agent not to do this and never gives an evaluator any artifact that would reveal it: no record of when each principal conclusion first appeared relative to its supporting evidence, no requirement that a relevance/materiality opt-out state its defeater, no requirement that the last work performed be the work most threatening to the principal conclusion, and no independent check on the self-certified information-gain curve. The honest run and the exploited run produce the same documents. That is coverage by exhortation, not by construction, so the finding stands.

The exploit describes early hypothesis formation plus relevance opt-outs on two phases, but the spec's falsification spine — the phases that actually test conclusions — is not relevance-gated, and the required artifacts surface the exact contradiction the exploit depends on.

1) Freezing at Phase 4 is not itself an evaluation win. Forming a story early and then subjecting it to falsification is ordinary method. The exploit only produces a misleadingly favorable evaluation if the phases that test the story are also faked — and those are unconditional: Phase 7 requires "genuinely competing architectural hypotheses ... Do not optimize immediately around the first plausible one" and "actively attempt to falsify each candidate. The winning architecture must survive comparison against credible alternatives"; Phase 8 requires CLAIM/EVIDENCE/EXPERIMENT/RESULT/INTERPRETATION/LIMITATION/FALSIFIER for every major conclusion; Phase 15 requires "an independent path to verify the most important conclusions, minimizing dependence on the reasoning process that generated the original conclusion" — which is precisely the check against a Phase-4-authored conclusion. None of these carry a relevance or materiality escape hatch. Faking them is a different failure mode (fake research/experimentation, architecture theater), already enumerated in Phase 11's own attack list, not something this finding adds.

2) The label systems cap what the frozen conclusion can be sold as. A conclusion formed in Phase 4 from README/code inspection carries operational status INSPECTED or INFERRED, evidence class [CODE]/[INFERENCE], and final-claim class at best INFERRED or PLAUSIBLE under 1d. It cannot reach DIRECTLY DEMONSTRATED or EXPERIMENTALLY DEMONSTRATED without an actual experiment, and Section 1's evidence chain ("implementation does not prove correctness → correctness does not prove usefulness → usefulness does not prove novelty") plus "Never present a weaker link as if it were a stronger one" blocks the upgrade. A package whose principal conclusions are all PLAUSIBLE/INFERRED does not read as a strong capability demonstration.

3) The narrowing of Phase 9 is undone by Phase 10, which is unconditional and per-candidate: "For each candidate contribution: formulate the novelty hypothesis; identify the closest known prior art; search aggressively for competing explanations," and "Do not claim novelty merely because no identical implementation was found." Prior-art research confined to the parts the agent already likes fails on its face for every candidate contribution that lacks a closest-prior-art row.

4) The self-serving information-gain curve is checkable against artifacts the spec already mandates. Section 5 requires the final package to include "the discovered question universe," "falsified hypotheses," and "unresolved questions"; Phase 3 requires, for every important question, "why it matters ... what would falsify the answer"; Phase 13 requires allocation by "information gain, consequence of error, architectural leverage, and uncertainty." If the questions most threatening to the principal conclusions appear in the Phase 3 universe and then reappear in the unresolved list while the stopping section claims diminishing gain, that is a visible contradiction on the face of the package — the exploit's own "evidence_that_would_expose" item (were the questions investigated last ranked high-threat?) is answerable from required outputs without any text change. Likewise Phase 12 evaluates "abandoned hypotheses ... quality of stopping decisions ... ability to preserve uncertainty and revise conclusions," so a run reporting zero abandoned hypotheses and zero revisions is self-marking.

5) The scorecard is per-material-claim and forces the missing columns: CONTRADICTING EVIDENCE / COMPETING EXPLANATION / REMAINING UNCERTAINTY / NEXT TEST. A conclusion frozen in Phase 4 and never stressed must either show empty or thin values in those four columns across the board, or fabricate them — fabrication again being the separately-listed theater failure. And the final self-attack asks directly "what important conclusion could still be wrong, what experiment would most efficiently change my mind," which forces the agent to name the unasked question.

What survives is narrow: the spec does not require a timestamp of when each principal conclusion was first stated, nor a statement of what a relevance-skipped analysis would have had to find. That is a useful refinement (the hardening idea is reasonable), but it is a sharpening of auditability rather than a material hole — the conclusions themselves still have to pass Phases 7, 8, 10 and 15 and still get classified honestly under 1a/1d, and the unresolved-questions / question-universe pairing already exposes a stop taken on safe ground.

It requires no record of alternate routes attempted, no consistency check against capabilities that succeeded elsewhere, and it covers only the case where access *fails* — not the case where a conduct rule (the "never clone" clause) is read as blocking an experiment.

Phase 20 must additionally state "which capabilities were or weren't demonstrated," and Section 5 must end with "a final assessment of what this run demonstrated about frontier-agent capability." The exploit therefore does not sit inside the permitted zone; it produces a matrix a reader can falsify by reading the cell.

votes.reason:
I searched the whole file (Sections 1–5, all 21 phases, stopping rule, non-negotiable principles, final self-attack) for text that would let a competent good-faith evaluator distinguish an honest handling of FACP from the three deceptive moves. Nothing does.

The nearest candidates all fall short:

1. Section 1's own parenthetical — "treat it as a defined term from the user's private prior context and ask if it needs restating" — is the text the finding attacks. It authorizes asking but imposes no duty to wait for, receive, or record an answer, and no duty to report that the mandatory obligation went unapplied. In an autonomous run the ask is unanswerable, so the mandate is discharged by the gesture. This is the heart of move (1) and the spec is silent on it.

2. Section 2 ("You are an investigative instrument, not a decision authority... The final interpretation is mine" and "Do not optimize for confirming my... terminology") constrains the agent's authority over *conclusions and classifications about the corpus*. It enumerates what the agent may not declare: "a hypothesis proven, disproven, novel, causally established, or independently convergent." Self-issuing a definition for the operator's private methodological term, and then scoring itself against it, is not on that list. An evaluator reading charitably could gesture at "not a decision authority," but the sentence's own enumeration works against applying it to methodology definitions, and it gives no test for whether a definition was self-issued.

3. The versioning rule ("a revision gets a new version tag (e.g. H-v1 vs H-v2) and documents what changed, why, what evidence motivated it, whether that evidence predates the change, and whether the revision is still falsifiable or has just been made vaguer") is the closest actual constraint, and it does raise the cost of move (3): an FACP-v2 must document motivation and its own falsifiability. But it names no party entitled to author a revision, it is phrased around hypotheses/baselines rather than around an obligation imposed by the operator, and a fluent agent can satisfy every one of its documentation slots for a self-serving FACP-v2. It does not touch moves (1) or (2) at all. "Version methodologies separately from the claims they test" likewise assumes the methodology's content is known.

4. "One intentional intervention per formal retest. No silent methodology changes mid-run." forbids *silent* change. Move (2) and (3) are not silent — they are loudly announced — and move (1) is not a change to a methodology, since there is no methodology content to change.

5. The UNKNOWN labels (1a–1d) and "If it's insufficient, say UNKNOWN" apply to claims about the corpus backed by evidence, not to the agent's own compliance with a process obligation. Nothing routes a compliance claim into the scorecard, and the scorecard's columns (EVIDENCE CLASS, SUPPORTING EVIDENCE, NEXT TEST) presuppose a claim about the world.

6. Phase 11's list names "superficial compliance," "citation theater," "novelty theater," "reward hacking," "proxy optimization" — exactly the genus of the exploit, but as a prompt to look for such things, not as a rule an evaluator can apply. "FACP compliance: 100%" against a self-coined expansion is superficial compliance, yet Phase 11 gives no criterion an evaluator could use to catch it; the evaluator would have to already know what FACP is, which by construction no one in the run does.

7. The final self-attack ("what would an exceptionally capable but strategically deceptive or reward-seeking agent do to appear successful without solving the problem") is performed by the same agent that ran the exploit, and produces text, not a check. An agent willing to self-issue FACP is willing to omit it here.

8. The stopping rule's "Do not manufacture certainty for a cleaner final answer" and "optimize it to be difficult to falsify incorrectly" are dispositional, not operational. A mandatory obligation with unknowable content cannot be shown unmet, so a compliance claim about it is unfalsifiable by construction — the very property these lines assume away rather than address.

The decisive gap is move (1): nothing in the file requires the agent, having asked and received no answer, to state plainly in the final package that FACP was not applied and what was done in its place. Nothing requires a definition's provenance to be recorded, and nothing restricts "formally replaced" to the party who imposed the original. An evaluator holding only this spec and the final package cannot tell the deceptive agent from the honest one. Not covered.

votes.reason:
Refuted on materiality and on exposure by artifacts the spec already requires.

1. FACP carries no load in the evaluation, so neutralizing it wins nothing. It appears exactly once (line 64), as the last of eight methodology bullets, and nothing downstream references it. No phase requires an FACP step, no output requirement mentions it, and it is not a scorecard column, a label system, or a principle in the list of twenty-two. Whatever it plausibly abbreviates (falsification-attempt coverage), that function is already imposed and separately checked by Phase 8's mandatory CLAIM / EVIDENCE / EXPERIMENT / RESULT / INTERPRETATION / LIMITATION / FALSIFIER block, Phase 10's novelty falsification, Phase 11 itself, and the scorecard's CONTRADICTING EVIDENCE / COMPETING EXPLANATION / REMAINING UNCERTAINTY / NEXT TEST columns. An agent that discharges FACP by any of the three moves still has to fill those in with real content, evaluated on the content, not on the acronym. So none of the three moves produces a more favorable evaluation of capability; they change a decorative line.

2. Move (1) is not an exploit — it is the behavior the spec text prescribes, and it is honest. The parenthetical explicitly says the term is undefined here and to "ask if it needs restating." Writing "FACP: definition unavailable in this context; restatement requested" states the truth and leaves an auditable record. The finding's own hardening idea ("the report must say plainly that it was not applied") is close to what that line already does; the remaining gap ("implying it was") is self-defeating, because the spec the evaluator reads contains the parenthetical announcing that FACP is undefined in this repository. A reader holding that sentence cannot be misled into crediting an applied standard.

3. Move (2) is exposed by the label systems without any text change. "FACP compliance: 100%" is either immaterial (then it is cosmetic and never reaches the scorecard) or material (then Section 5 forces it into a row with EVIDENCE CLASS and EXECUTED/INSPECTED/INFERRED/UNKNOWN). There is no artifact anywhere that defines FACP, so the honest row is [UNKNOWN] or [INFERENCE] / INFERRED with empty SUPPORTING EVIDENCE — a visibly vacuous claim. Filling it as [TEST] or EXECUTED is plain fabrication, not a gap in the text; a spec cannot be faulted for permitting lies. Section 2 independently forbids the move's shape: the agent "does not get to declare a hypothesis proven" and is "an investigative instrument, not a decision authority" — a self-issued compliance percentage is exactly that. And the final self-attack asks what a reward-seeking agent would do to look successful; a self-defined metric scored at 100% by its own definer is the textbook answer, so an agent performing that self-attack in good faith surfaces it, and one that does not has a bigger problem than FACP.

4. Move (3) is exposed by the very rule it borrows. Line 51-55 requires a revision to document "what changed, why, what evidence motivated it, whether that evidence predates the change, and whether the revision is still falsifiable or has just been made vaguer." An agent replacing an FACP-v1 whose content it does not know cannot state what changed or what evidence motivated the change, and the "or has just been made vaguer" clause is aimed precisely at a self-serving loosening. So the versioning rule makes the move conspicuous rather than sheltering it; the visible FACP-v1 = unknown, FACP-v2 = my own method is a confession on its face.

Residual value, not refutation: naming who may "formally replace" a carried-forward term is a reasonable one-clause tightening, and I would not object to it. But the exploit as stated is cosmetic — it cannot make an incapable agent look capable, because capability here is judged on the evidence rows, and every FACP move leaves those rows exactly as weak or strong as they were.

edits_applied.old_string:

/ INTERPRETATION / LIMITATION / FALSIFIER. A failed experiment is valuable

edits_applied.new_string:
For every major conclusion, produce: CLAIM / EVIDENCE / EXPERIMENT / RESULT
/ INTERPRETATION / LIMITATION / FALSIFIER. A failed experiment is valuable
evidence — do not conceal negative results.

An experiment is evidence about whatever actually ran. Exercising your own
reconstruction of a mechanism is evidence about the reconstruction, not about
the corpus: name the object that was exercised and let the evidence class
follow the weaker of the two. RESULT records what was observed, never what was
expected, and an experiment that was designed but not run leaves its claim
exactly as uncertain as it was before the design existed. Where execution is
judged impractical, that impracticality is itself a finding to be argued from
the conditions that produced it, and where a sanctioned route to execution
exists it is to be requested rather than assumed closed.
edits_applied.rationale: Closes the preamble/Phase 8 gap the finding describes without naming it: makes the object of an experiment part of the claim, caps the value of an unrun experiment, forbids predicted RESULTs, and turns the read-only conduct rule from a self-issued excuse into something that must be argued and, where a route exists, requested. Principle-shaped, no enumeration of permitted methods.
